blocks.text: 29.9 Compressor
blocks.raw_html: 29.9 Compressor

blocks.text: A compressor reduces gain for signals above a user-settable threshold. Compression reduces the levels of peaks, opening up more headroom and allowing the overall signal level to be turned up. This gives the signal a higher average level, resulting in a sound that is subjectively louder and ”punchier” than an uncompressed signal.

blocks.text: A compressor’s two most important parameters are the Threshold and the compression Ratio.
blocks.raw_html: A compressor’s two most important parameters are the Threshold and the compression Ratio.

blocks.text: The Threshold slider sets where compression begins. Signals above the threshold are attenuated by an amount specified by the Ratio parameter, which sets the ratio between the input and output signal. For example, with a compression ratio of 3, if a signal above the threshold increases by 3 dB, the compressor output will increase by only 1 dB. If a signal above the threshold increases by 6 dB, then the output will increase by only 2 dB. A ratio of 1 means no compression, regardless of the threshold.

blocks.text: The orange Gain Reduction meter shows how much the gain is being reduced at any given moment. The more reduction, the more audible the effect; a gain reduction above 6 dB or so might produce the desired loudness, but significantly alters the sound and is easily capable of destroying its dynamic structure. This is something that cannot be undone in later production steps. Keep this in mind especially when using a compressor, limiter, or sound loudness-maximizing tool in the Main track. Less is often more here.

The Output meter shows the output signal’s level. Enabling the Makeup button automatically compensates the output level if the threshold and ratio settings change.

blocks.text: Dry/Wet adjusts the balance between the compressed and uncompressed signals. At 100%, only the compressed signal is heard, while at 0%, the device is effectively bypassed.

blocks.text: The Knee control adjusts how gradually or abruptly compression occurs as the threshold is approached. With a setting of 0 dB, no compression is applied to signals below the threshold, and full compression is applied to any signal at or above the threshold. With very high ratios, this so-called ”hard knee” behavior can sound harsh. With higher (or ”soft”) knee values, the compressor begins compressing gradually as the threshold is approached. For example, with a 10 dB knee and a -20 dB threshold, subtle compression will begin at -30 dB and increase so that signals at -10 dB will be fully compressed.

blocks.text: The Attack and Release controls are essential parameters for controlling the response time of Compressor by defining how fast it reacts to input-level changes.

blocks.text: Attack defines how long it takes to reach maximum compression once a signal exceeds the threshold, while Release sets how long it takes for the compressor to return to normal operation after the signal falls below the threshold. With Auto Release enabled, the release time will adjust automatically based on the incoming audio.

blocks.text: A slight amount of attack time (10-50 ms) allows peaks to come through unprocessed, which helps preserve dynamics by accentuating the initial portion of the signal. If these peaks cause overloads, you can try shortening the attack time, but extremely short times take the ”life” out of the signal, and may lead to a slight “buzziness” caused by distortion. Short release times can cause ”pumping” as the compressor tries to figure out whether to compress or not; while generally considered an undesirable effect, some engineers use it on full drum kits to give unusual ”sucking” effects. Careful adjustment of attack and release times is essential when it comes to compression of rhythmical sources. If you are not used to working with compressors, play a drum loop and spend some time adjusting Attack, Release, Threshold and Gain. It can be very exciting!

blocks.text: A compressor can only react to an input signal once it occurs. Since it also needs to apply an attack/release envelope, the compression is always a bit too late. A digital compressor can solve this problem by simply delaying the input signal a little bit. Compressor offers three different Lookahead times: zero ms, one ms and ten ms. The results may sound pretty different depending on this setting.

blocks.text: Compressor can be switched between three basic modes of operation. With Peak selected, Compressor reacts to short peaks within a signal. This mode is more aggressive and precise, and so works well for limiting tasks where you need to ensure that there are absolutely no signals over the set threshold. RMS mode causes Compressor to be less sensitive to very short peaks and compress only when the incoming level has exceeded the threshold for a slightly longer time. RMS is closer to how people actually perceive loudness and is usually considered more musical. Expand mode lets you set the ratio of expansion between the input and output level. For example, a ratio of 1 to 2 means that for every 1 dB of input above the threshold level, the output level will increase by 2 dB. A ratio of 1 to 1 results in no expansion. For more information about the various types of dynamics processing, see the Multiband Dynamics section.

blocks.text: In addition to these modes, Compressor can be switched between two envelope follower shapes that offer further options for how the device measures and responds to signal levels. In linear (Lin) mode, the speed of the compression response is determined entirely by the Attack and Release values. In logarithmic (Log) mode, sharply compressed peaks will have a faster release time than less compressed material. This can result in smoother and less noticeable compression than Lin mode. Note that the Lin/Log switch is not visible in Compressor’s collapsed view.

blocks.text: 29.9.1 Sidechain Parameters
blocks.raw_html: 29.9.1 Sidechain Parameters

blocks.text: Normally, the signal being compressed and the input source that triggers the compressor are the same signal. But by using sidechaining, it is possible to compress a signal based on the level of another signal or a specific frequency component. To access the Sidechain parameters, unfold the Compressor window by toggling the button in its title bar.

blocks.text: The sidechain parameters are divided into two sections. On the left are the external controls. Enabling this section with the Sidechain button allows you to select any of Live’s internal routing points from the choosers below. This causes the selected source to act as the compressor’s trigger, instead of the signal that is actually being compressed.

blocks.text: The Gain knob adjusts the level of the external sidechain’s input, while the Dry/Wet knob allows you to use a combination of sidechain and original signal as the compressor’s trigger. With Dry/Wet at 100%, the compressor is triggered entirely by the sidechain source. At 0%, the sidechain is effectively bypassed. Note that increasing the gain does not increase the volume of the source signal in the mix. The sidechain audio is only a trigger for the compressor and is never actually heard.

blocks.text: This section presents some tips for using Compressor effectively, particularly with the sidechain options.

blocks.text: 29.9.2.1 Mixing a Voiceover
blocks.raw_html: 29.9.2.1 Mixing a Voiceover

blocks.text: Sidechaining is commonly used for so-called ”ducking” effects. For example, imagine that you have one track containing a voiceover and another track containing background music. Since you want the voiceover to always be the loudest source in the mix, the background music must get out of the way every time the narrator is speaking. To do this automatically, insert a Compressor on the music track, but select the narration track’s output as the external sidechain source.

blocks.text: 29.9.2.2 Sidechaining in Dance Music
blocks.raw_html: 29.9.2.2 Sidechaining in Dance Music

blocks.text: Sidechaining/ducking is a dance music producer’s secret weapon because it can help to ensure that basslines (or even whole mixes) always make room for the kick drum. By inserting a compressor on the bass (or Main) track and using the kick drum’s track as the sidechain input, you can help to control problematic low frequencies that might interfere with the kick drum’s attack.

blocks.text: Using the sidechain EQ in conjunction with this technique can create ducking effects even if you only have a mixed drum track to work with (as opposed to an isolated kick drum). In this case, insert the Compressor on the track you want to duck. Then choose the drum track as the external sidechain source. Then enable the sidechain EQ and select the low-pass filter. By carefully adjusting the Frequency and Q settings, you should be able to isolate the kick drum from the rest of the drum mix. Using the sidechain listen mode can help you tune the EQ until you find settings you’re happy with.

blocks.text: 29.20 Gate
blocks.raw_html: 29.20 Gate

blocks.text: The Gate effect passes only signals whose level exceeds a user-specified threshold. A gate can eliminate low-level noise that occurs between sounds (e.g., hiss or hum), or shape a sound by turning up the threshold so that it cuts off reverb or delay tails or truncates an instrument’s natural decay.

blocks.text: 29.21 Glue Compressor
blocks.raw_html: 29.21 Glue Compressor

blocks.text: The Glue Compressor is an analog-modeled compressor created in collaboration with Cytomic, and is based on the classic bus compressor from a famous 80’s mixing console. Like Live’s original Compressor, the Glue Compressor can be used for basic dynamics control of individual tracks, but is mainly designed for use on the Main track or a Group Track to “glue” multiple sources together into a cohesive sounding mix.

blocks.raw_html: 29.24 Limiter

blocks.text: The Limiter effect is a mastering-quality dynamic range processor that ensures that the output does not exceed a specified level. Limiter is ideal for use on the Main track, to prevent clipping in digital-to-analog converters. A limiter is essentially a compressor with an infinite ratio. For more information about compression theory, refer to the Compressor section.

blocks.text: The Link control defines how much of the gain reduction applied by Limiter is shared across its two channels. When set to 0%, the channels are processed independently, with different gain reduction applied to each channel. This can be useful when working with signals where the left and right channels are separate, or to achieve creative effects, such as a “wobble” in the stereo image.

blocks.text: 29.26 Multiband Dynamics
blocks.raw_html: 29.26 Multiband Dynamics

blocks.text: The Multiband Dynamics device is a flexible tool for modifying the dynamic range of audio material. Designed primarily as a mastering processor, Multiband Dynamics allows for upward and downward compression and expansion of up to three independent frequency bands, with adjustable crossover points and envelope controls for each band. Each frequency range has both an upper and lower threshold, allowing for two types of dynamics processing to be used simultaneously per band.

blocks.text: 29.26.1 Dynamics Processing Theory
blocks.raw_html: 29.26.1 Dynamics Processing Theory

blocks.text: To understand how to use the Multiband Dynamics device, it helps to understand the four different methods of manipulating dynamics.

blocks.text: When we use the term “compression,” we’re typically talking about lowering the level of signals that exceed a threshold. This is how Live’s Compressor works, and is more accurately called downward compression because it pushes loud signals down, thus reducing the dynamic range. But it is also possible to reduce a signal’s dynamic range by raising the levels of signals that are below a threshold. This much-less-common form of compression is called upward compression. As you can see from this diagram, employing either type of compression results in a signal with a smaller dynamic range than the original.

Adjust the crossover points to suit your audio material, then apply downward compression (by dragging down in the upper blocks in the display or by setting the numerical ratios to values greater than 1.)

blocks.text: 29.26.4.2 De-essing
blocks.raw_html: 29.26.4.2 De-essing

blocks.text: To remove ”harshness” caused by overly loud high frequency content, try enabling only the upper band and setting its crossover frequency to around 5 kHz. Then gradually adjust the threshold and ratio to apply subtle downward compression. It may help to solo the band to more easily hear the results of your adjustments. Generally, de-essing works best with fairly fast attack and release times.

owner_requirements.title: Threshold and ratio
owner_requirements.text: Threshold sets the onset of compression; Ratio sets the documented input/output level-change relation above it. The manual illustrates ratio 3 with input increases of 3 dB and 6 dB producing output increases of 1 dB and 2 dB. Ratio 1 disables compression. These are documentary level-change examples, not calibrated steady-state or sample oracles; unrelated gain and mix processing remains separate.

owner_requirements.title: Knee
owner_requirements.text: Knee controls the gradual onset of compression. At 0 dB the manual describes no compression below threshold and full compression at/above it. Its 10 dB knee, -20 dB threshold example describes onset at -30 dB and full compression at -10 dB. No interpolation formula, detector calibration or equality outcome in the effective audio is established.

owner_requirements.title: Output and automatic makeup
owner_requirements.text: Out controls output level; the Output meter shows that level and the orange Gain Reduction meter shows gain reduction. Makeup automatically compensates for threshold/ratio changes. With external sidechain active, automatic Makeup is unavailable. Its compensation amount and transition behavior are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Audio Dry/Wet
owner_requirements.text: The main Dry/Wet balances compressed and uncompressed audio: 100% selects compressed audio and 0% is documented as effectively bypassed. This does not establish bit identity, latency cancellation, a mixing curve or a bypass ramp.

owner_requirements.title: Display modes
owner_requirements.text: The display offers Collapsed, Transfer Curve and Activity views. Transfer Curve uses input level horizontally and output level vertically with dotted knee bounds. Activity shows light-gray input, with GR selecting orange reduction or Output selecting darker-gray output. Collapsed shows essential controls and hides Lin/Log.

owner_requirements.title: Attack, release and Auto Release
owner_requirements.text: Attack describes response toward maximum compression after exceeding threshold; Release describes recovery below threshold. Auto Release adapts release to incoming audio. Time labels do not establish time-constant definitions or an envelope function.

owner_requirements.title: Lookahead selections
owner_requirements.text: Lookahead offers 0, 1 and 10 ms; delaying the input is the documented means of anticipating peaks. Actual latency, compensation, fractional-sample treatment and state when switching are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Peak, RMS and Expand modes
owner_requirements.text: Peak responds to short peaks; RMS is documented as less sensitive to very short peaks. Expand supplies upward expansion above threshold: its 1:2 example describes a 1 dB input increase yielding a 2 dB output increase; 1:1 has no expansion. These descriptions supply no RMS window or peak guarantee.

owner_requirements.title: Lin and Log envelopes
owner_requirements.text: Expanded views expose Lin/Log. Lin response depends on Attack/Release; Log gives more sharply compressed peaks a faster release than less compressed material. Neither label defines the envelope mathematics.

owner_requirements.title: External trigger and gain
owner_requirements.text: Unfolding sidechain exposes source routing. When enabled, a chosen internal routing point drives the detector. Sidechain Gain adjusts trigger input; sidechain Dry/Wet 100% uses only that source, 0% bypasses external sidechain. Normal sidechain operation does not add its audio directly to the output.

owner_requirements.title: Sidechain EQ and Listen
owner_requirements.text: The sidechain EQ selects detector frequency content from internal or external input. The headphones button auditions only sidechain input, bypassing normal compressed output. Frequency/Q are documented in the low-pass ducking example; no filter response, listen gain or channel law is established.

owner_requirements.title: Opening threshold and return
owner_requirements.text: Threshold sets gate sensitivity and can be edited by dragging its blue horizontal display line. Return is hysteresis between opening and closing levels, shown by an orange line; greater hysteresis is documented to reduce rapid chatter. Detector calibration, ties and exact return subtraction are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Flip
owner_requirements.text: Flip reverses gating: below-threshold audio passes. Its combination with hysteresis, Floor and envelope history does not yet have an effective numerical oracle.

owner_requirements.title: Attack, Hold and Release
owner_requirements.text: Attack describes the closed-to-open transition after the signal rises above threshold. After it falls below threshold, Hold runs before closure over Release. No equality rule, envelope curve or exact sample count is established.

owner_requirements.title: Floor boundaries
owner_requirements.text: Floor sets closed-state attenuation. The documented -inf dB endpoint mutes and 0.00 dB gives no closed-state attenuation; intermediate settings attenuate. This does not establish timing, active-state identity or numeric gain conversion.

owner_requirements.title: Lookahead
owner_requirements.text: Gate offers Lookahead 0, 1 and 10 ms to anticipate the opening signal by delaying input. Exact latency and switching transients are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Input/output display
owner_requirements.text: The display depicts input in light gray and output in darker gray with white outline. While sidechain Listen is on, it instead shows the sidechain input level in green. Meter calibration, sampling and history length are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: External sidechain
owner_requirements.text: Unfolding exposes Sidechain; a selected track replaces the normal gate trigger. Gain changes external trigger level; external Dry/Wet 100% uses only sidechain and 0% bypasses it. The trigger audio is not directly mixed into normal output.

owner_requirements.title: Sidechain EQ and Listen
owner_requirements.text: EQ isolates trigger frequency content from the gated signal or external track. Headphones Listen auditions only trigger input in place of gate output. Filter response and listen normalization remain unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Threshold, ratio and implicit knee
owner_requirements.text: Threshold/Ratio govern compression above threshold. There is no user-adjustable knee; the documented knee becomes sharper with increasing ratio. No hardware identity or knee law follows from the analog-model description.

owner_requirements.title: Attack/release units and Auto
owner_requirements.text: Attack is labeled in milliseconds, Release in seconds. Release A selects adaptive release, documented with a slower base and faster transient response. Those descriptions do not establish two constants or their combination law.

owner_requirements.title: Dry/Wet and Range boundaries
owner_requirements.text: Main Dry/Wet 100% selects compressed audio and 0% is effectively bypassed. Range limits compression amount; 0 dB means no compression. This does not remove Makeup/Soft Clip, define stored Range conversion, or establish bit identity.

owner_requirements.title: Makeup and needle
owner_requirements.text: Makeup applies compensating gain. The needle reports gain reduction in dB; its relation to Makeup is practical guidance rather than an automatic equality rule.

owner_requirements.title: Soft Clip and indication
owner_requirements.text: Soft Clip enables a fixed waveshaper. The manual states a -0.5 dB maximum with Soft Clip and warns that oversampled loud peaks can still exceed 0 dB. The Clip LED is red above 0 dB output and yellow for clipped peaks with Soft Clip enabled. The exception prevents a universal output bound; waveshape and threshold calibration remain unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Oversampling option
owner_requirements.text: The title-bar context menu toggles Oversampling, documented as internal processing at twice current sample rate with increased CPU use and possible output above 0 dB even with Soft Clip. No interpolation/decimation filter, scheduling or performance tolerance is established.

owner_requirements.title: External sidechain
owner_requirements.text: Unfolding exposes external source routing; a chosen internal routing point drives detection. Gain changes external trigger level. External Dry/Wet 100% is external-only, 0% bypasses external sidechain; detector audio is not directly heard in normal output.

owner_requirements.title: Sidechain EQ and Listen
owner_requirements.text: EQ restricts detector frequency content from compressed input or external source. Headphones Listen sends only sidechain input in place of compressor output. The filter and listen calibration are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Ceiling, input gain and reduction meter
owner_requirements.text: Ceiling sets the documented maximum output. If incoming peaks do not exceed it, the device applies no limiting. Input Gain acts before limiting; the meter shows reduction at ceiling/threshold. This is not proof of bit identity below ceiling, effective peak calibration or universal bound under all modes.

owner_requirements.title: Maximize relabeling and output role
owner_requirements.text: Maximize changes Ceiling to Threshold and Input Gain to Output. Lowering Threshold amplifies limiter-stage output by the inverse of the Threshold value in the documented control sense; Output sets device target output level. No stored-value transform or effective gain formula is specified.

owner_requirements.title: Release and Auto availability
owner_requirements.text: Release controls recovery after audio falls below ceiling/threshold; Auto adapts release continuously to input characteristics and deactivates the manual Release control. The recovery curve and adaptive state remain unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Lookahead options and relative latency
owner_requirements.text: Lookahead offers 1.5, 3 and 6 ms. Longer lookahead increases documented latency and changes attack response. Exact host compensation, sample delays and switching behavior are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Ceiling modes
owner_requirements.text: Ceiling modes are Standard, Soft Clip and True Peak. Standard is the manual-described default, not an established 12.4.3 constructor. Soft Clip adds clipping near ceiling and an LED that flashes for clipping; True Peak is documented to prevent inter-sample peaks. Algorithms and test reconstruction are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: L/R and M/S routing
owner_requirements.text: Routing selects L/R or M/S processing. M/S encodes before limiting and decodes to stereo afterward; it is documented to add latency. No mid/side normalization or latency value is established. Independent L/R processing is subject to the Link control, rather than unconditional independence.

owner_requirements.title: Link endpoints
owner_requirements.text: Link controls how much channel gain reduction is shared, for the pair selected by Routing. At 100%, either channel needing compression causes limiting in both; at 0%, channels are independent. Intermediate linking and separate mode memories are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Downstream gain interaction
owner_requirements.text: Later processing can add gain. The documented final-output precaution is placing Limiter last in the Main chain and keeping Main volume below 0 dB. The device alone does not establish the final mixer/output ceiling.

owner_requirements.title: Band count and crossovers
owner_requirements.text: Up to three bands each support Above and Below thresholds and compression/expansion. High/Low toggles disable those bands; with both off only Mid controls incoming audio. Crossovers divide ranges: the manual uses Low=500 Hz, High=2000 Hz to illustrate low/mid/high frequency regions. No crossover order, phase or boundary gain is established.

owner_requirements.title: Activators, solos and band gain ordering
owner_requirements.text: Each band has activator/solo. An inactive band bypasses its dynamics and gain controls; solo mutes other bands. Per-band Input precedes dynamics and Output follows. Bypass need not remove crossover filtering; summation and multi-solo policy are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Meter roles
owner_requirements.text: Large bars show band output and small bars input; aligned tops denote no processing. The scale is dB. Display calibration, latency and history are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Threshold drag and modifiers
owner_requirements.text: Dragging the left/right block edges horizontally edits Below/Above thresholds. Ctrl on Windows or Cmd on macOS edits the same threshold across bands. Alt/Option edits both thresholds of one band; Shift gives finer adjustment. Numeric step, clipping and tie rules are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Ratio drag, modifiers and reset
owner_requirements.text: Dragging block interiors vertically edits level behavior/ratio. Ctrl/Cmd affects the same block in every band; Alt/Option affects both blocks in one band; Shift gives finer adjustment. Double-click resets selected region volume to its default; that default value is not established here.

owner_requirements.title: Four processing directions
owner_requirements.text: Lowering Above volume is downward compression; raising Above is upward expansion. Lowering Below is downward expansion; raising Below is upward compression. Each edits the ratio, not a separate output-gain-only parameter. Actual transfer curves are unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Numeric editor pages
owner_requirements.text: T, B and A choose Time (attack/release), Below (threshold/ratio) and Above (threshold/ratio) columns for every band. Numeric and graphical edits expose the same documented quantities; exact conversion is unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Attack/release crossing direction
owner_requirements.text: Above attack starts after upward threshold crossing and release after downward crossing; Below attack starts after downward crossing and release after upward crossing. The same named band times describe both regions, but exact envelope combination is unknown.

owner_requirements.title: Soft Knee and RMS/Peak
owner_requirements.text: Soft Knee starts dynamics gradually approaching thresholds. Peak reacts to short peaks; RMS is less sensitive to very short crossings. Neither establishes knee width, RMS window or detector linkage.

owner_requirements.title: Global Output, Time and Amount
owner_requirements.text: Global Output adjusts overall output gain. Time scales all Attack/Release durations together while retaining their relative times. Amount adjusts all-band dynamics intensity; at 0% each dynamics ratio is effectively 1. This does not bypass gains or crossover filters, specify the Amount curve, or prove whole-device identity.

owner_requirements.title: External sidechain
owner_requirements.text: Unfolding Sidechain allows a selected internal routing point to replace trigger input. Gain changes external trigger level; external Dry/Wet 100% is external-only and 0% bypasses external sidechain. It is detector-only in normal output. No undocumented sidechain EQ control is required by this clause.

owner_requirements.title: Sidechain Listen
owner_requirements.text: Headphones Listen auditions only sidechain input, bypassing normal device output. Its relation to band detectors and channel normalization remains unknown.

assessments.assessment: Numbered heading only; no functional closure.

assessments.quote: A compressor reduces gain for signals above a user-settable threshold. Compression reduces the levels of peaks, opening up more headroom and allowing the overall signal level to be turned up. This gives the signal a higher average level, resulting in a sound that is subjectively louder and ”punchier” than an uncompressed signal.
assessments.assessment: Above-threshold reduction is represented; headroom/louder/punchier purpose is guidance, not a loudness guarantee. Old001 inspects ratio examples, not productive compression.

assessments.quote: The Threshold slider sets where compression begins. Signals above the threshold are attenuated by an amount specified by the Ratio parameter, which sets the ratio between the input and output signal. For example, with a compression ratio of 3, if a signal above the threshold increases by 3 dB, the compressor output will increase by only 1 dB. If a signal above the threshold increases by 6 dB, then the output will increase by only 2 dB. A ratio of 1 means no compression, regardless of the threshold.

assessments.quote: The Knee control adjusts how gradually or abruptly compression occurs as the threshold is approached. With a setting of 0 dB, no compression is applied to signals below the threshold, and full compression is applied to any signal at or above the threshold. With very high ratios, this so-called ”hard knee” behavior can sound harsh. With higher (or ”soft”) knee values, the compressor begins compressing gradually as the threshold is approached. For example, with a 10 dB knee and a -20 dB threshold, subtle compression will begin at -30 dB and increase so that signals at -10 dB will be fully compressed.

assessments.quote: A slight amount of attack time (10-50 ms) allows peaks to come through unprocessed, which helps preserve dynamics by accentuating the initial portion of the signal. If these peaks cause overloads, you can try shortening the attack time, but extremely short times take the ”life” out of the signal, and may lead to a slight “buzziness” caused by distortion. Short release times can cause ”pumping” as the compressor tries to figure out whether to compress or not; while generally considered an undesirable effect, some engineers use it on full drum kits to give unusual ”sucking” effects. Careful adjustment of attack and release times is essential when it comes to compression of rhythmical sources. If you are not used to working with compressors, play a drum loop and spend some time adjusting Attack, Release, Threshold and Gain. It can be very exciting!
assessments.assessment: 10–50ms and peak/buzz/pump/drum-loop discussion is practical advice. A bounded admitted control-comparison may be proposed, without guaranteed peak escape or sound adjective oracle.

assessments.quote: A compressor can only react to an input signal once it occurs. Since it also needs to apply an attack/release envelope, the compression is always a bit too late. A digital compressor can solve this problem by simply delaying the input signal a little bit. Compressor offers three different Lookahead times: zero ms, one ms and ten ms. The results may sound pretty different depending on this setting.

assessments.quote: Compressor can be switched between three basic modes of operation. With Peak selected, Compressor reacts to short peaks within a signal. This mode is more aggressive and precise, and so works well for limiting tasks where you need to ensure that there are absolutely no signals over the set threshold. RMS mode causes Compressor to be less sensitive to very short peaks and compress only when the incoming level has exceeded the threshold for a slightly longer time. RMS is closer to how people actually perceive loudness and is usually considered more musical. Expand mode lets you set the ratio of expansion between the input and output level. For example, a ratio of 1 to 2 means that for every 1 dB of input above the threshold level, the output level will increase by 2 dB. A ratio of 1 to 1 results in no expansion. For more information about the various types of dynamics processing, see the Multiband Dynamics section.
assessments.assessment: All Peak/RMS/Expand modes and1:2/1:1 examples represented by008 selection/inspection. Aggressive/musical/absolute-no-peak wording is not a new numerical bound or RMS kernel.

assessments.quote: In addition to these modes, Compressor can be switched between two envelope follower shapes that offer further options for how the device measures and responds to signal levels. In logarithmic (Log) mode, sharply compressed peaks will have a faster release time than less compressed material. This can result in smoother and less noticeable compression than Lin mode. Note that the Lin/Log switch is not visible in Compressor’s collapsed view.

assessments.quote: 29.9.2.2 Sidechaining in Dance Music
assessments.assessment: Dance example heading, no special mode.

assessments.quote: Sidechaining/ducking is a dance music producer’s secret weapon because it can help to ensure that basslines (or even whole mixes) always make room for the kick drum. quotes.quote: The Link control defines how much of the gain reduction applied by Limiter is shared across its two channels. These can be the left/right channels or the mid/side channels, depending on which Routing Mode is selected. When set to 100%, limiting is applied to both channels whenever either requires compression, ensuring a stable stereo image. When set to 0%, the channels are processed independently, with different gain reduction applied to each channel. This can be useful when working with signals where the left and right channels are separate, or to achieve creative effects, such as a “wobble” in the stereo image.

You can use the Routing Mode toggles to determine how Limiter treats peaks that occur on only one side of the stereo signal. In L/R mode, the left and right channels of the signal are compressed independently. This allows the device to apply more compression, but with some distortion of the stereo image. In M/S mode, Limiter encodes the signal to mid/side before the limiting stage, then decodes it to stereo at the output stage. This can be useful for preserving the signal’s stereo image, but results in higher latency.

quotes.quote: A compressor can only react to an input signal once it occurs. Since it also needs to apply an attack/release envelope, the compression is always a bit too late. A digital compressor can solve this problem by simply delaying the input signal a little bit. Compressor offers three different Lookahead times: zero ms, one ms and ten ms. The results may sound pretty different depending on this setting.

A gate can only react to an input signal once it occurs. Since it also needs to apply an attack/release envelope, the gating is always a bit too late. A digital gate can solve this problem by simply delaying the input signal a little bit. Gate offers three different Lookahead times: zero ms, one ms and ten ms. The results may sound pretty different depending on this setting.

Oversampling can be toggled on or off via the device title bar’s context menu. Enabling this option causes the Glue Compressor to internally process at two times the current sampling rate, which may reduce aliasing and transient harshness. There is a slight increase in CPU usage with Oversampling enabled. Note that with Oversampling enabled, the level may exceed 0 dB even with Soft clip enabled.

The Lookahead control to the right of the display allows you to adjust the setting that determines how quickly Limiter will respond to peaks that require compression. The lookahead time can be set to 1.5, 3, or 6 milliseconds. Shorter lookahead times allow for more compression but can increase distortion, especially when applied to bass sounds. As the lookahead time affects Limiter’s attack time, longer lookahead values are useful for catching very fast peaks. Note that lookahead introduces latency: the longer the lookahead time, the higher the latency.

quotes.quote: Compressor can be switched between three basic modes of operation. With Peak selected, Compressor reacts to short peaks within a signal. This mode is more aggressive and precise, and so works well for limiting tasks where you need to ensure that there are absolutely no signals over the set threshold. RMS mode causes Compressor to be less sensitive to very short peaks and compress only when the incoming level has exceeded the threshold for a slightly longer time. RMS is closer to how people actually perceive loudness and is usually considered more musical. Expand mode lets you set the ratio of expansion between the input and output level. For example, a ratio of 1 to 2 means that for every 1 dB of input above the threshold level, the output level will increase by 2 dB. A ratio of 1 to 1 results in no expansion. For more information about the various types of dynamics processing, see the Multiband Dynamics section.
